title: Dipa Ma
hookLine: the Indian laywoman who lost her family, found peace through meditation, and taught many

lines: A WHITE SARI, A SMALL APARTMENT.
ONCE TOO WEAK TO CLIMB THE STEPS.
cards: A small woman in a white sari sits in a cramped apartment in Calcutta. Her visitors are students, neighbors, sometimes Westerners who've traveled a long way. She isn't a nun.

She has no temple. She cooks, looks after her grandson, and teaches meditation from the floor of her home. Years earlier, people who knew her say, grief had left her so weak she could barely climb the steps of a temple.
How did she get from there to here?

teach.h: NANI BALA BARUA, CALLED DIPA MA.
teach.b: Her name was Nani Bala Barua, and people came to call her Dipa Ma, mother of Dipa, after her daughter. She grew up in a Buddhist family in Bengal, married, and moved with her husband to Burma.
Then the losses came, one after another, as her students tell it: children who died, and then her husband. She was left with her young daughter Dipa, with grief, and with a failing body.
A doctor, the story goes, told her that her real illness was sorrow, and that she should learn to meditate. So she went to a meditation center in Rangoon. The early days were hard.

teach.h: CRAWLING UP THE STAIRS TO PRACTICE.
teach.b: On her way there, her students say, she would stop and stop, and finally crawl up the stairs. But she kept going.
She practiced noting, naming each movement of body and mind as it happened, and over time, they say, the grief loosened its hold and her health came back.

Later she taught in Calcutta, mostly householders like herself: mothers, workers, people who couldn't leave for a monastery. Some of the teachers who later brought insight meditation to the West studied with her.
What she told them was plain.
Practice in the kitchen: while you cook, while you wash, while you look after a child. You don't need a cave. And notice the order of the story.
She didn't heal first and then practice. She practiced while she was broken, and rebuilt from there, one noted step at a time.

how: Insight meditation teachers often tell Dipa Ma's story as an example of a householder's practice, and some retreat centers and sitting groups encourage people to bring noting into chores, cooking and caring for family.

games.q: you're Dipa Ma, so weak with grief you can hardly climb the stairs to the meditation hall. what do you do?
o: wait at home until you're stronger
crawl up the stairs and practice
send your daughter in your place
games.why: her students say she crawled up the steps and kept practicing, and the healing came through the practice, not before it.

practice: Bring to mind someone who went through something hard and slowly put a life back together: a grandparent, a friend, a neighbor, maybe you.

Don't retell the whole story; just picture them on an ordinary day afterward, making breakfast, laughing at something small, and let the respect be quiet. If your mind drifts, note it, wandering, and come back to their face.

wordCard.voice: Dipa Ma. A laywoman who practiced through grief, rebuilt her life, and taught householders to meditate right where they lived.

carryVoice: Your line: she rebuilt. Practice can start in the kitchen, even on a broken day. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Accounts of Dipa Ma's life by her students (e.g. Amy Schmidt, Dipa Ma: The Life and Legacy of a Buddhist Master)
